newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.African shares shunned as banks lift rates.
newsitem.headline: S.African shares shunned as banks lift rates.

text.p: South African share prices tumbled on Thursday as the country's leading commercial banks followed the lead of the central Reserve Bank, hiking their prime lending rates by one point to 20.25 percent.
At midday the Johannesburg Stock Exchange's (JSE) all-share index was off 1.05 percent at 6,779.3 as investors took fright from a move that will apply the brakes to an already faltering economy.

But the country's battered currency took heart from the move, which increases returns on rand deposits, firming nearly four cents to around 4.62 against the U.S. dollar, dragging government bond prices up in its wake.
Stock market analysts said stores would be particularly hard hit in the vital run-up to Christmas with many consumers already struggling to service their borrowings at previous interest rates.
Retail shares were among the biggest losers on the JSE with the sub-index off 1.7 percent.
Denzil Newman, portfolio manager at Syfrets Managed Assets Ltd, said there was likely to be an overall de-rating of South African stocks -- but he did not foresee a price crash.

"It probably means P/Es (price/earnings ratios) can get down to the 12 to 13 area from the current 15. But you are still getting reasonably good growth from some companies, so prices may be flattish," he said.
"We don't see a major crash. The market probably has a maximum 10 percent downside."
Reserve Bank Governor Chris Stals announced the one point increase to 17 percent in the key Bank rate, at which it lends overnight to commercial banks, on Wednesday night.
Stals said the move was necessary given an unstable rand, rising short-term money market rates and the threat of higher inflation.
Economists said his decision showed he was determined to crack down on inflation -- which hit a 16-month high of 9.1 percent in October -- despite the pain this would cause.

Forecasts of growth in 1997 had already been coming down and many analysts are now expecting growth of only some two percent next year, down from around 3.0 percent this year and a seven-year high of 3.3 percent achieved in 1995.

Share dealers said the JSE was likely to be nervous in the coming days and weeks, although some held out hopes that bargain-hunters would come in soon, given the widening price differential with runaway Wall Street stocks.
"There is a chance it could firm a tad. It will near levels where shares will start to look cheap," one dealer said.

One sector which should have taken heart from the rate increase was the banking sector, since higher prime will go some way to relieve an acute squeeze on margins caused by an unseasonally high money market shortage.
In fact, bank shares fell along with the rest of the market and analysts said the banks were still set for tough trading conditions.
"Even with a 100-basis point hike, they (banks) are still bleeding compared to where they have been," said one analyst who asked not to be identified.
